summary:
SPHEREx Viewer is a free public website that turns NASA's SPHEREx archive into a short movie of the sky. Pick a challenge target or type any coordinate, and it shows real SPHEREx images of that patch of sky epoch by epoch, aligned on a common grid. Blink and Difference modes, like the comparator that found Pluto, make whatever moved or changed brightness stand out while the static sky disappears.

A Python pipeline queries IRSA, removes zodiacal light, discards bad pixels, aligns hundreds of exposures and stacks them per epoch. The site also builds each target's 0.75-5 µm spectrum from individual exposures, overlays Gaia DR3 and AllWISE on an all-sky map, and offers false color, shareable links and a Portuguese/English interface.

All five challenge targets pass an automated science validation against SIMBAD and Gaia: WISE 0855 appears only at 4-5 µm and moves as predicted, Barnard's Star's motion is measured to 0.02 pixel, and both variable stars change brightness at over 12 sigma. Data refresh every three days and are published only if validation passes.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, but comparing its images takes expert skills. SPHEREx Viewer lets anyone look for the next moving dot.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Viewer turns NASA's SPHEREx archive into a short movie of the sky. You pick one of the challenge targets or type any coordinate (degrees or sexagesimal) or an object name, and the site shows real SPHEREx images of that patch of sky, one frame per epoch, aligned on a common grid. A fixed crosshair and a circle at the catalog-predicted position guide the eye. Four modes help you compare: Play (the epochs in order), Blink (two epochs back and forth, like the comparator Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto), Difference (one epoch minus another, in units of noise, so the static sky disappears and only what changed remains) and Sum (all epochs stacked for depth). You can switch between the six detectors (0.75 to 5 µm), use false color (D6, D3, D1 as red, green, blue), mark unreliable pixels, choose a 6′ or 10′ field, and share the exact view through the URL or embed it in another page.

For each challenge target the site also shows a 0.75 to 5 µm spectrum built from individual exposures (each SPHEREx exposure sees the target through a different part of its linear variable filter) and warns when a neighbor star falls inside the measurement aperture. An all-sky SPHEREx map, with Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays, answers "is this dot already known?" and opens any spot in the viewer.

How it works

A Python pipeline queries the IRSA archive (TAP, with SIA as a fallback), downloads a cutout of every exposure, subtracts the zodiacal light, discards bad pixels using the quality flags in two levels, reprojects everything onto one tangent-plane grid with normalized interpolation, groups exposures into epochs and stacks each epoch with inverse-variance weights. The output is a small, formal data contract (JSON Schema): a field.json plus float32 frames of about 14 KB each. The browser does contrast, blinking, differencing and stacking locally, so changing modes needs no new requests.

The five challenge targets are pre-processed in 6′ and 10′ and published as static files, so they open instantly. Any other coordinate goes to a FastAPI service that processes the field on demand and reports progress while it downloads. A GitHub Actions workflow refreshes the targets every three days with new SPHEREx data, runs a scientific validation against independent catalogs, and publishes only if it passes.

Results and benefits

All five challenge targets pass the automated validation (16 tests on real data, checked against SIMBAD and Gaia DR3):

  • WISE 0855 appears only at 4 to 5 µm, at the predicted position (0.12 to 0.19 px).
  • Barnard's Star moves about 11″ north in a year, measured to about 0.02 px.
  • Epsilon Indi B is detected at S/N 250 to 640, and its motion matches.
  • RW Aurigae brightens 1.35× between epochs (12σ), and R Draconis fades to 0.46× (15σ).
  • Field stars stay put to 0.02 to 0.04 px: the alignment is about 25 times better than a pixel.

The benefit is access. Seeing what moved in SPHEREx data used to require querying an archive, reading FITS files and aligning hundreds of rotated images. Now it takes a browser and a few seconds, for a student, an amateur astronomer or a researcher who wants a quick look.

Intended impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is far more sky than professional astronomers can inspect by eye. Citizen-science projects such as Backyard Worlds have shown that volunteers comparing images find real brown dwarfs and moving objects. SPHEREx Viewer brings that method to a new mission in the infrared, where cold, nearby objects shine, and makes it easy to share a candidate with a single link. It is also a teaching tool: Pluto's discovery method, live, with today's data.

Tools and technologies

  • Python 3.12 with Astropy, reproject and NumPy (pipeline); FastAPI (API); uv for environments.
  • TypeScript with Vite, no UI framework; Vitest for tests; Aladin Lite for the all-sky map.
  • JSON Schema as the contract between backend and frontend.
  • GitHub Pages (site), Render free tier (API), GitHub Actions (automatic updates and tests).
  • Data: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images and the all-sky HiPS cube from NASA/IPAC IRSA; SIMBAD; Gaia DR3 and AllWISE via VizieR.
  • Development was test-driven: 192 automated tests, including the scientific validation. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for coding, documentation and review.
  • No special hardware: a laptop and free cloud services.

What makes it creative

  • It treats the archive as a time-lapse, in the spirit of Tombaugh's blink comparator, and keeps that metaphor in the design: epochs are shown like glass photographic plates, with red pencil marks for the predicted position.
  • It uses the 102 bands creatively: stacking all exposures of a detector per epoch for depth, false color from three detectors, and a spectrum assembled from exposures that each sample a different wavelength.
  • The Difference mode is expressed in units of noise, not raw brightness, so what stands out is statistically real change.
  • Coordinates from another epoch (like the 2010 position of WISE 0855 in the challenge text) are recognized and open the object where it is today.

Factors we considered

  • People without astronomy training: a plain-language introduction and "how to read" steps at the top, target descriptions written for non-experts with a "what to look for" hint, a dark-sky default, and the interface in English and Portuguese.
  • Scientific honesty: positions propagated by proper motion, quality flags shown instead of hidden, warnings when a neighbor star contaminates the spectrum, and a validation that blocks publication if the science fails.
  • Reliability: the IRSA services went down during the hackathon, so the pipeline falls back from TAP to SIA, retries with backoff, skips and reports single failed exposures, and never caches a transient error.
  • Cost and maintenance: everything runs on free tiers, with no database; new SPHEREx releases are a configuration change.
  • Speed: challenge targets are pre-processed and served as static files; the browser handles all interaction.
  • Openness: open source under GPL-3.0, shareable links and embed mode so results can be cited and reused.
